CRD: All comparable experimental units enter one common randomization pool.
RCBD: Comparable units are first grouped into blocks; treatments are randomized within each block.

CRD: Treatments are randomly assigned across all eligible units.
RCBD: Each treatment appears within every complete block.

CRD: No formal blocking; relies more heavily on unit comparability and randomization.
RCBD: Explicitly controls one important source of nuisance variation represented by the blocks.

CRD: Useful when dealer-period units are sufficiently homogeneous.
RCBD: Useful when product, dealer, market or comparable-period differences are expected to affect demand.

CRD: Simple to design, randomize and explain.
RCBD: Can reduce unexplained variation and improve treatment comparison when blocks are meaningful.

CRD: Product, dealer, market or timing differences may increase unexplained variation.
RCBD: Requires well-defined blocks and can become difficult if units or treatments are unavailable within blocks.

CRD: Experimental units should be sufficiently comparable and treatment assignment must be genuinely random.
RCBD: Blocks should be internally comparable and all treatments should be implementable within each complete block.

CRD: Must be managed if customers, dealers or promotions affect nearby units.
RCBD: Still possible; randomization and operational separation must prevent contamination between treatments.

CRD: Potentially feasible for a small pilot with clearly separated comparable units.
RCBD: Potentially feasible, but requires more coordination, scheduling and record keeping than CRD.
